title: Front-end architecture for offline, real-time and AI apps

labels.seq: A user action through the layers
labels.tech: Choices and when to pick them

summary: In data-heavy mobile and web apps, the front end is not a thin skin. It owns the source of truth the user sees, the state machine of every screen, perceived performance, offline behaviour, real-time updates, streaming AI output and accessibility. Principal-level answers describe these layers as precisely as the backend.
does: Render immutable UI state derived from a local source of truth
Model each screen as a small state machine with explicit loading, empty, error, offline and pending states
Own perceived performance: startup, scrolling, image and video memory
Handle offline, retries and conflicts visibly and honestly
Integrate real-time sockets and streaming AI responses smoothly
Meet accessibility and localisation requirements by default
doesnt: Call the network from views or composables
Keep business rules in UI code
Block the main thread with parsing, hashing or database work
Hide failures behind infinite spinners
Encode meaning with colour alone
scenario: Take the job detail screen in the inspection app. When it opens, the ViewModel subscribes to a database query for the job, its answers and its media. The first frame renders from SQLite in about 50 ms, before any network activity.

The technician changes an answer. The ViewModel sends an intent to the repository, which writes the answer and an outbox row in one transaction. The query emits again, the reducer produces a new immutable state with that field marked pending, and Compose recomposes only that row.

In the background, the sync engine pushes the change and the server returns the supervisor’s edit to the instructions. The same query emits again; the instructions update in place and a small ‘Updated by Priya’ label fades in. No screen code knows the network exists.

If the push returns a conflict, the row’s state becomes conflict, the reducer maps it to an amber badge, and tapping it navigates to the resolver. Every one of these states was designed, named and screenshot-tested before the feature shipped.
archNotes: Unidirectional data flow

Views send intents; a ViewModel or store reduces intents and data changes into one immutable state object; views render it. This is MVI on Android, the same shape with @Observable models or TCA on iOS, and a Zustand or Redux store in React.
Observe, don’t fetch
Screens subscribe to database queries. Network results are written to the database, which updates the screen. That gives offline support, instant reopening and one source of truth.
Effects
One-off events such as navigation, toasts and haptics are separate from state, so rotating the device or recomposing does not repeat them.
Real-time and streaming
Sockets and server-sent events are data sources like any other: they write to the database (chat) or to a stream buffer (AI tokens) that the reducer consumes.
Design system
Tokens and components with accessibility built in. Screens compose components; they don’t restyle them.
states: The four base states every list screen must design.
Per-row sync states for offline-first data.
Show the change immediately and reconcile when the server answers.
Placeholder shapes that match final layout, used only on first load.
Show cached data, refresh in the background, update in place.
A double tap produces the same result as a single tap.

Feature flags · server-driven UI · OTA for JS (EAS Update)

Dropped or slow frames during scroll
Smoothness on real devices, not flagships.

Should be one frame for local writes.
Share of screens shown from cache

Configuration change repeats a toast or navigation
Model one-off effects separately from state.
Stable keys, reserved image sizes, and insert-above only on user request.
Thousands of rows update at once during sync
Batch database writes per page so observers emit once.
Buffer tokens and render in 50 ms batches; re-parse only the last paragraph.
Right-to-left and large fonts break layouts
Screenshot tests in those variants; avoid fixed heights for text.
interview: How do you structure a screen in an offline-first app?

Unidirectional data flow: the view sends intents; the ViewModel writes through a repository and observes database queries; a reducer produces immutable state with explicit loading, empty, error, offline and per-row sync states; effects are separate.
How do you make a list of 10,000 items smooth on a cheap phone?
Paged reads from the local database, virtualisation with stable keys and content types, flat item layouts, images decoded to display size off the main thread, and production frame metrics.
How do you design for failure in the UI?

Every async state is named and designed: pending, failed with a reason and retry, conflict with a resolver, offline with a count. No infinite spinners, and nothing claims success before the source of truth confirms it.
What changes in the front end when you add AI?
Streaming rendering with buffering, visible tool progress, structured action cards for confirmations, cancel and retry, feedback capture tied to prompt versions, and a non-AI fallback path.

title: The sync engine
summary: The sync engine is a small runtime inside the app with one job: move local changes to the server and server changes into the local database. It has no UI and no business logic beyond merging. It must be safe to start, stop and kill at any line, because the OS will do all three.
does: Drain the outbox in order, in batches, with op_ids
Pull changes after the stored cursor, page by page
Apply each page and save the cursor in one transaction
Run conflict rules and mark rows that need the user
Respect a time budget and report a result to the scheduler
Emit metrics for every run
doesnt: Decide when to run (the background-work layer does)
Move file bytes (the transfer manager does)
Render anything or hold UI state
Keep state in memory between runs
Trust the device clock for ordering
scenario: Priya, a field technician, edits twelve inspection jobs in a basement with no signal. Every save writes the job row and an outbox entry in one SQLite transaction, so the app feels instant. Meanwhile two supervisors change instructions on two of those same jobs from the office.

At 4:12 pm she walks outside. The phone regains a network, WorkManager’s network constraint is met, and the scheduler calls run(reason = network_back, budget = 8 minutes). The coordinator takes the single-flight lock and reads the cursor c_88411 from disk.

The push stage reads 37 outbox operations, sends them in two batches of up to 25, and gets back 36 applied and 1 conflict: the supervisor changed the same ‘valve 3 status’ field. Acknowledged operations are deleted and their rows marked synced in the same transaction; the conflicting row is marked conflict with the server’s value attached.

The pull stage asks for changes after c_88411, receives 140 changes in one page, applies them in a single transaction and stores c_88551. The run takes 2.1 seconds, emits a trace, and returns success. Priya sees eleven green ticks and one amber ‘needs review’ badge with both values side by side.
archNotes: Coordinator

Entry point. Takes a single-flight lock so two triggers never run two syncs, computes a deadline from the budget, runs push then pull, and maps exceptions to a result the scheduler understands: success, retry after N seconds, needs login, or disabled.
Push stage
Reads the next batch of outbox rows that are ready (not waiting for a retry time), serialises them with op_ids and base versions, and handles each per-operation result inside one transaction.
Pull stage
Loops over pages from the stored cursor until the server says has_more is false or the deadline arrives. A 410 Gone response switches it to the rebuild path.
Merge policy
Pure functions, one per entity type, that decide what to do when a server change meets a row with pending local edits. Pure functions make this the easiest part to unit test.
Applier
Writes a page of changes in one transaction: inserts, updates, deletes from tombstones, and the new cursor. Observers fire once per page, not once per row.
HTTP client and auth
A shared client with timeouts, gzip, HTTP/2 and an authenticator that refreshes tokens once and retries. If refresh fails, the run ends with needs login and sync pauses.
states: Nothing running. Waiting for a run request.
Last run failed with a retryable error; next attempt not before a jittered time.
Token refresh failed. Sync pauses until the user signs in.
Cursor too old (410). Push outbox, keep unsynced rows, import snapshot.
Remote kill switch on. Runs return immediately.

msgs: Loop until has_more = false or the budget ends

seqNotes: Every arrow that changes local state ends in a transaction, so the run can be killed between any two arrows without losing or duplicating data.
Push always runs before pull, so the server’s answer already reflects this device’s edits.
The result tells the scheduler what to do next, which keeps retry policy in one place.
code: Applying one change with pending local edits
Staying inside the OS time budget (Kotlin)
platforms: Android
Engine in a Kotlin module with no Android UI dependencies, so it is unit-testable on the JVM.
Room DAOs with withTransaction for every state change; WAL is on by default.
OkHttp with an Authenticator for token refresh, gzip and HTTP/2; Retrofit or Ktor on top.
A CoroutineWorker calls run() with a budget of a few minutes and maps the result to Result.success() or Result.retry().
iOS
A Swift package with the engine as an actor, so state is never touched from two tasks at once.
GRDB DatabasePool in WAL mode; write transactions for every state change.
A default URLSession for API calls (they are short); background sessions are for big files only.
BGAppRefreshTask gives about 30 seconds, so the budget is around 25; BGProcessingTask allows longer runs while charging.
React Native
The engine stays native and is exposed through a Turbo Module with requestSync(reason) and a status observable.
JavaScript reads the same SQLite database through WatermelonDB or op-sqlite and re-renders on change.
No sync logic in JavaScript, because the JS runtime may not exist when the OS wakes the app.
Shared core (KMP)
Engine in commonMain with SQLDelight for the database and Ktor for HTTP.
expect/actual for the scheduler hooks, crypto and clocks.
One test suite runs the protocol against a fake server for both platforms.
tech: Local database
Room · GRDB · SQLDelight · WatermelonDB · op-sqlite
Room or GRDB natively; SQLDelight for KMP; WatermelonDB for RN with its sync protocol.
Wire format
JSON + gzip · Protobuf (Wire, swift-protobuf)
Start with JSON; switch hot endpoints to Protobuf when payloads or parse time hurt on low-end phones.
Transport
HTTPS request/response · WebSocket hint channel · gRPC
HTTPS for push and pull; a socket only to say ‘cursor moved’ while the app is open.
Off-the-shelf sync
PowerSync · ElectricSQL · Replicache / Zero · Couchbase Lite · Firestore offline
Buy when sync is not your differentiator; build when you need custom merge rules, residency or evidence guarantees.
Testing
Fake server · property-based tests · fault injection
Generate random sequences of edits, kills and network failures and assert convergence.
real: Dropbox
Publicly described rewriting its desktop sync engine, Nucleus, in Rust, with heavy use of deterministic and randomised testing to find rare sync bugs.
Linear
Has described a client that keeps a local copy of workspace data, applies changes optimistically, and receives ordered changes from the server tracked by an increasing sync ID.
Figma
Has described a server-authoritative multiplayer model where clients send property-level changes and the server resolves conflicts per property.
Replicache (Rocicorp)
Documents a push/pull protocol where each client mutation carries an ID and the server records the last processed mutation ID per client, which is the op_id pattern.
metrics: Slow runs hit OS budgets and get cancelled.
The single best indicator users are seeing stale data.
Growing values mean pushes are failing silently.
Spikes in rejected or conflict usually mean a bug, not users.
Too many pages means devices sync too rarely; 410s mean TTL is too short.
Shows which triggers actually deliver fresh data.
edges: SQLite rolls back; the batch is pushed again and deduped by op_id.
Retry returns DUPLICATE with the original result; row marked synced.
Pulled change for a row with pending edits
Merge policy runs; unresolved fields become a conflict for the user.
Delete arrives for a row edited offline
Marked conflict instead of deleting the user’s work.
Clock on the phone is wrong
Ordering comes from server sequence numbers; local timestamps are display-only.
Schema of a pulled change is newer than the app
Unknown fields are kept as raw JSON and preserved on push; never dropped.
interview: Why is the engine single-flight?
Two concurrent runs could push the same outbox rows twice and apply pages out of order. A lock plus idempotent server writes keeps one logical sync at a time.
Why push before pull?
So the server’s view, which the pull returns, already includes this device’s edits, and the merge only has to handle edits made by others.
How do you test a sync engine?
Pure merge functions with unit tests, the engine against a fake server, and randomised fault injection: random edits, kills between transactions, dropped responses, then assert all replicas converge.
What happens if the OS cancels the run halfway?
Nothing is lost. Every step committed atomically, the cursor only moves with its page, and the next run continues from disk.

title: The transfer manager
summary: The transfer manager moves large files between the phone and object storage. It hashes, splits, uploads and downloads files in parts that each succeed or fail on their own, records progress after every part, and keeps going across network switches, app kills and reboots.
does: Copy the source into app storage and hash it while copying
Ask the server whether the content already exists
Plan parts and upload several in parallel
Persist each part’s ETag the moment it lands
Refresh expired URLs and resume after any interruption
Download with Range requests, verify and rename atomically
doesnt: Sync records (the sync engine does)
Decide product rules like Wi-Fi only (it reads them as constraints)
Hold file bytes in memory or in JavaScript
Trust a file path that the system can revoke
scenario: Arjun records a 412 MB walkthrough video of a pump room and taps Submit. The transfer manager copies the file into app storage while computing its SHA-256, so it reads the file once. It asks the server with POST /files/init; the hash is new, so the server starts a multipart upload and returns 52 presigned part URLs of 8 MB each, valid for 15 minutes.

Four parts upload at a time. After each one, the ETag goes into the transfer_part table. At part 20 the phone moves from Wi-Fi to 4G: three in-flight parts fail, retry after a short jittered delay and succeed. At part 31 the URLs have expired, the server returns 403, and the manager asks for fresh URLs for parts 31 to 52 only.

Arjun’s phone is an iPhone and he swipes the app away at part 38. iOS cancels the background transfers. When he opens the app an hour later, the manager reads the table, sees 37 parts done, requests URLs for parts 38 to 52 and finishes. It then sends POST /files/complete with all 52 part numbers and ETags; the server verifies the hash and links the video to the inspection.
Total bytes re-sent because of the network switch and the swipe: about 32 MB out of 412 MB. Without part checkpoints, the swipe alone would have cost 296 MB.
archNotes: Public API
enqueue(uri, owner, priority) returns a transfer ID immediately; observe(id) streams progress from the database; cancel(id) marks it cancelled so nothing restarts it.
Preparer

Copies the file into app storage, because content URIs and photo-library references can disappear, and computes SHA-256 in the same pass. Optional transcoding happens here, before any bytes leave the phone.
Part planner
Chooses part size from file size and network: at least 5 MB (the S3 minimum for all but the last part), usually 8–16 MB, and large enough to stay under 10,000 parts.
URL broker
Owns the upload ID and presigned URLs. It refreshes URLs in bulk when they are near expiry or a PUT returns 403, so expiry never fails a transfer.
Worker pool
Runs two to four part uploads concurrently, fewer on cellular or low battery. It records each part’s ETag in its own small transaction.
Downloader
Uses Range requests to resume, writes to a temporary file, verifies the hash, and renames into place so a half-written file is never visible.
states: Accepted and persisted. Waiting for constraints such as Wi-Fi or charging.
Asking the server whether the content already exists.
Parts in flight; progress = parts done ÷ total.
System stopped us, network lost, or constraints no longer met. Resumes automatically.
All parts done; asking the server to assemble and verify.
Linked to its record. Local copy can be evicted later.
Permanent error such as file deleted or hash mismatch; shown to the user.
User cancelled. Server multipart upload aborted.

msgs: Wi-Fi → 4G at part 20: in-flight parts retry

seqNotes: The hash is computed once, during the copy, and reused for deduplication and final verification.
Each part commits independently, so any interruption costs only the parts in flight.
Expired URLs are a normal event, refreshed in bulk, never a failure.
code: Streaming one part without loading it (OkHttp)
Android: one WorkManager job per part
platforms: Android
WorkManager unique work per transfer (upload- plus the ID) with network and battery constraints for background priority.
For uploads the user started, a user-initiated data transfer job on Android 14 and later, with a progress notification and cancel action.
OkHttp with a FileSliceBody so memory stays flat regardless of file size.
Media3 Transformer for on-device video compression before upload.

Background URLSession with one upload task per part file; the system keeps transferring while the app is suspended.
handleEventsForBackgroundURLSession in the app delegate, and the stored completion handler called after events are delivered.
BGContinuedProcessingTask (iOS 26+) or a short background task for the hashing and compression step.
AVAssetExportSession for video compression.
React Native
A native module with enqueueUpload(uri, priority) that returns a transfer ID; progress is read from SQLite.
Pass file URIs only; bytes never enter the JS heap.
react-native-background-upload or a custom module wrapping the native pieces above.
tech: Upload protocol
S3 multipart with presigned URLs · GCS resumable uploads · Azure block blobs · tus
Use your cloud’s native protocol; tus when you need a vendor-neutral, open resumable protocol.
Integrity
SHA-256 of the whole file · per-part checksums (S3 supports CRC32C, SHA-256 and others)
Whole-file hash for dedupe and evidence; per-part checksums to catch corruption in transit.
Concurrency
1 · 2–4 · adaptive
Two on cellular, four on Wi-Fi; drop to one when the battery is low.
Compression
Media3 Transformer · AVAssetExportSession · none
Compress video when the product allows; never re-compress photos used as evidence.
Download delivery
CDN signed URLs · direct storage URLs
CDN with content-addressed keys for anything downloaded more than once.
real: Google APIs
Publish a resumable upload protocol: create an upload session, send the file in chunks, and query the server for how many bytes it received before resuming.
tus
An open protocol for resumable uploads over HTTP, with server and client libraries in many languages; Vimeo is among its well-known adopters.
Dropbox API
Exposes upload sessions (start, append, finish) so large files are sent in pieces and committed at the end.
Amazon S3
Multipart upload: up to 10,000 parts, each at least 5 MB except the last, assembled by a final complete call; incomplete uploads should be cleaned up with a lifecycle rule.
metrics: The headline number: share of enqueued files that reach done.
Shows whether checkpoints and part size are working.
403 expiry, timeouts and 5xx need different fixes.
How often uploads were skipped because the server already had the bytes.
Transfers stuck paused for days usually mean a missing constraint or a killed OEM job.
edges: Source file deleted or permission revoked
Already copied into app storage at enqueue time, so the transfer continues.
Hash mismatch on complete; transfer marked failed and re-enqueued from the new file.
403 triggers a bulk refresh for remaining parts; not counted as a failure.
Refuse new copies with a clear message; evict uploaded files first.
Server treats complete as idempotent by upload ID.
Storage lifecycle rule aborts incomplete multipart uploads after a few days.
interview: Why copy the file before uploading?
Picker and gallery URIs can be revoked or the user can edit the photo. A private copy with a recorded hash is the only stable source for a transfer that may take hours.
How do you choose part size?

Big enough to keep request overhead low and stay under the part limit, small enough that a lost part is cheap on cellular. 8 MB on cellular and 16 MB on Wi-Fi is a sensible start; measure resend ratio.
Why not one background task for the whole file on iOS?
If it fails at 90%, you restart from zero. One task per part gives checkpoints that survive relaunch.
How do you prevent duplicate storage when users re-upload?
Content addressing: the server looks up the SHA-256 at init and links the existing object.

title: The background-work layer
summary: The background-work layer is a thin adapter between your app and the OS scheduler. It turns many triggers (app open, network back, push, timers, user actions) into a few well-behaved jobs, gives each job a time budget, and hands results back to the OS so it keeps trusting your app.
does: Collect triggers and coalesce them into one job
Map jobs to WorkManager on Android and BGTaskScheduler on iOS
Pass a time budget and a cancellation signal to the engines
Translate engine results into success, retry or reschedule
Record which triggers actually ran, per OS and manufacturer
doesnt: Contain sync or transfer logic
Keep anything alive with wake locks or endless services
Poll the server on a timer while the app is closed
scenario: In one minute, Meera’s phone produces five reasons to sync: she edits a booking, the app goes to the background, Wi-Fi reconnects, a push arrives saying her clinic changed a time, and the periodic job comes due. A naive app would start five syncs.

The trigger hub coalesces them. On Android, each trigger enqueues unique work named sync with a KEEP policy, so only one job exists. On iOS, the edit starts a short background task to finish the write, and the rest schedule one app refresh request.

WorkManager runs the job when the network constraint is met. The worker calls the sync engine with an eight-minute budget. The engine returns Success with more pending, so the worker returns success and enqueues one follow-up job.

Over a week, telemetry shows that on one manufacturer’s phones, periodic jobs ran 70% less often. The team adds a one-time battery-settings guide for affected users and shifts weight to sync-on-open, without touching the sync engine.
archNotes: Trigger hub

Accepts trigger(reason, priority). It collapses duplicates within a short window and decides the job type: an immediate expedited job after a user edit, a constrained job for background catch-up, or a user-initiated transfer job.
Android adapter

Enqueues unique work with WorkManager, sets constraints and backoff, uses expedited work with a fallback when quota runs out, and schedules user-initiated data transfer jobs for big uploads on Android 14+.
iOS adapter

Registers BGTask identifiers at launch, schedules BGAppRefreshTask and BGProcessingTask requests, wraps the expiration handler, and starts a short background task when the app is backgrounded mid-write.
Job runner
Creates a deadline from the OS budget, passes a cancellation token to the engines, and guarantees the OS is told the job finished.
Result mapper
Turns engine results into Result.success(), Result.retry() or setTaskCompleted(success:), and schedules the next run with the delay the engine suggested.
Run telemetry
Logs every run: trigger, scheduled time, actual start, duration, outcome, OS version and manufacturer. This is how you discover OEM restrictions.
states: A job exists with constraints; waiting for the OS.
Engine asked for a retry; OS backoff applies.
User or OS has stopped background work (Force Stop, background restrictions); runs only when the app opens.
seqNotes: Three triggers become one job because the work name is unique and the policy is KEEP.
Network work never happens inside the push callback; the callback only enqueues.
The worker always returns a result, so the OS keeps scheduling the app normally.
code: Android: periodic safety net and the leave-app trigger
platforms: Android
WorkManager for deferrable and expedited work; unique names stop duplicates.
User-initiated data transfer jobs for long uploads the user started (Android 14+).
Foreground services only with a declared type, and not as a long-term home for sync (Android 15 limits dataSync).
Test Doze with adb shell dumpsys deviceidle force-idle and standby buckets with am set-standby-bucket.
iOS
BGTaskSchedulerPermittedIdentifiers and UIBackgroundModes in Info.plist.
BGAppRefreshTask for short catch-up; BGProcessingTask for heavy work while charging.
Silent push only triggers a refresh; it is throttled and never guaranteed.
Simulate launches from the Xcode debugger with _simulateLaunchForTaskWithIdentifier.
React Native
A Turbo Module whose native side calls the same Android and iOS adapters.
expo-background-task or react-native-background-fetch for early versions, replaced by native adapters at scale.
JavaScript only requests work and observes results.
tech: Android scheduling
WorkManager · JobScheduler · AlarmManager · foreground service
WorkManager for almost everything; UIDT jobs for long user transfers; avoid exact alarms for sync.
iOS scheduling
BGTaskScheduler · background URLSession · silent push · beginBackgroundTask
Refresh tasks for catch-up, URLSession for bytes, short tasks to finish writes.
Push
FCM data messages · APNs background notifications
Use as a hint with collapse keys; never as the only path.
Cross-platform glue
Turbo Modules · Expo Modules API · KMP expect/actual
Turbo Modules for bare RN, Expo Modules in Expo apps, KMP for shared Kotlin.
metrics: runs per device per day by trigger
Reveals Doze, standby buckets and OEM throttling.
iOS schedules apps that overrun less often.
share of syncs on app open
If most syncs happen on open, background scheduling is not working for that segment.
edges: All jobs cancelled until the user opens the app; sync on open covers it.
User rarely opens the iOS app
Few background runs; push hints and on-open sync carry freshness.
Falls back to normal work automatically with the out-of-quota policy.
Collapse keys plus KEEP policy mean one job, not hundreds.
interview: Why put an adapter between engines and the OS?
The engines become platform-agnostic and testable, and all OS quirks, quotas and telemetry live in one small place per platform.
What do you do in the FCM callback?
Only enqueue work. The callback has a short time window, and the network call belongs in a worker with constraints and retries.
How do you know background sync works in the field?
Run telemetry by trigger, OS version and manufacturer, plus freshness percentiles. Without it, you are guessing.

title: The server sync service
summary: The server sync service is the other half of the protocol. It accepts pushes idempotently, applies merge rules, assigns every change a sequence number in a per-tenant change log, serves pulls by cursor with permission filtering, and builds snapshots for new devices.
does: Deduplicate pushes by op_id and return original results
Validate and merge changes per entity type
Write the entity and its change-log entry in one transaction
Serve ordered pages of changes after a cursor
Filter every pull by what the user may see
Publish changes for push hints, search and analytics
doesnt: Hold sessions or per-device state in memory
Order changes by client timestamps
Carry file bytes
scenario: A supervisor and a technician edit job j-81 within the same second. Both pushes reach different API pods. Each push is a transaction: check the op_id table, apply field-level merge against the current row, update the row, allocate the next sequence number for the tenant, and insert into the change log.

The technician’s push changes answers.valve_3 from base version 4. The supervisor changed only instructions. Both apply cleanly. Sequence numbers 88412 and 88413 are assigned. A third push, a retry of the technician’s request after a lost response, finds its op_id already recorded and returns the stored result without writing anything.

Debezium reads the change-log inserts from the Postgres write-ahead log and publishes them to Kafka. A notifier consumer coalesces them per user and sends one ‘changes available’ push to each affected device. A search consumer updates the index.

When the supervisor’s tablet pulls with cursor c_88411, the service returns rows 88412 and 88413 that her role may see, plus next_cursor c_88413. A tablet that has been off for 120 days asks with c_51200; that is older than the 90-day tombstone window, so it receives 410 and a snapshot URL.
archNotes: Push handler

For each operation: look up the op_id; if present, return the stored result. Otherwise load the row, run the entity’s merge rule, write the row, allocate a sequence and insert a change-log row, all in one transaction, then store the op_id result.
Change log

An append-only table keyed by (tenant_id, seq), partitioned by tenant hash and by time. Each row stores the entity, ID, version, changed fields or a tombstone flag, and the ACL tags needed to filter pulls.
Pull handler
A range read on (tenant_id, seq > cursor) ordered by seq, joined with the user’s permissions, limited by bytes as well as rows.
Snapshot builder
Builds a compressed SQLite file or NDJSON per scope from a consistent read at a known seq, uploads it to the CDN, and returns its seq as the starting cursor.
CDC to Kafka
Debezium streams committed change-log rows from the write-ahead log, so downstream consumers see exactly what was committed, in commit order.
states: Operation accepted and stored with a new sequence number.
op_id seen before; original result returned.
Base version stale on a field the server also changed; server values returned.
Validation or permission failure; client must not retry.
Cursor older than the tombstone window; client must rebuild from a snapshot.
seqNotes: The op_id check, the row update and the change-log insert share one transaction, so a retry can never create a second change.
Downstream systems read committed changes from the WAL rather than being called from the request path.
The other device learns about the change from a hint, but the pull is what guarantees it.
code:
CREATE TABLE change_log (
  tenant_id  bigint      NOT NULL,
  seq        bigint      NOT NULL,
  entity     text        NOT NULL,
  entity_id  uuid        NOT NULL,
  version    int         NOT NULL,
  fields     jsonb,                     -- changed fields; NULL for a tombstone
  deleted    boolean     NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
  acl        text[]      NOT NULL,      -- groups allowed to see this change
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, seq)
) PARTITION BY HASH (tenant_id);

CREATE TABLE processed_op (
  op_id uuid PRIMARY KEY, tenant_id bigint NOT NULL,
  result jsonb NOT NULL, created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);  -- purged after 14 days

CREATE TABLE tenant_seq (tenant_id bigint PRIMARY KEY, seq bigint NOT NULL);

SELECT seq, entity, entity_id, version, fields, deleted
FROM change_log
WHERE tenant_id = $1
  AND seq > $2                         -- the client's cursor
  AND acl && $3                        -- the user's groups
ORDER BY seq
LIMIT 500;
platforms: Service runtime
Node.js (Fastify or NestJS), Kotlin (Ktor) or Go; stateless pods behind a load balancer.
Connection pooling with PgBouncer; every request is one or a few short transactions.
Database
PostgreSQL with hash partitioning by tenant; Citus when a single node is no longer enough.
Per-tenant sequence rows serialise writers within a tenant, which is what keeps pull order safe.
Streaming
Debezium on the Postgres WAL into Kafka (or a managed equivalent); consumers for push hints, search, analytics and snapshots.
Edge
API gateway for auth and per-device rate limits; a CDN for snapshots and media.
tech: Sequence allocation
Per-tenant counter row · global sequence + watermark · WAL position (LSN)
Per-tenant counter for most products; a watermark when one tenant is too hot to serialise.
Change store
Postgres table · Cassandra/Scylla · DynamoDB stream
Postgres until write volume per tenant forces a wide-column store.
Idempotency store
Unique table in the same database · Redis
Same database when you need it inside the transaction; Redis as a fast front cache.
Change streaming
Debezium + Kafka · logical replication · application outbox
Debezium when you already run Kafka; an outbox table otherwise.
real: Replicache (Rocicorp)
Documents a pull that returns changes since a client’s cookie and a push that records the last processed mutation ID per client, the same idempotency idea as op_ids.
Linear
Has described tracking changes with an increasing sync ID so clients can request everything after the last ID they saw.
Debezium
An open-source change data capture platform that reads database write-ahead logs and publishes row changes to Kafka.
metrics: Duplicate share shows client retry health; conflict share shows product contention.
pull latency, rows and bytes per page
Large pages on mobile networks slow first sync.
Delays push hints and search updates.
How far behind devices are; tunes tombstone TTL.
Devices forced to rebuild; too high means TTL is too short.
edges: Two transactions allocate seq 10 and 11, 11 commits first

With a per-tenant counter row the second waits for the first, so commit order matches sequence order. With a global sequence, serve pulls only up to a safe watermark below the oldest in-flight transaction.
op_id lookup returns the stored result; no second change-log row.
User loses access to a record
Pull filters by current ACL; a revoke change tells devices to delete local copies.
Batch-allocate sequence ranges or split the tenant into scopes with their own counters.
interview: Why can a global sequence make pulls skip data?

Sequence numbers are allocated when a transaction asks for them, not when it commits. A later number can commit first, a client pulls past it, and the earlier one appears behind its cursor. Per-tenant serialisation or a safe watermark fixes it.
Where do you put the idempotency check?
In the same transaction as the write, so the check and the write cannot be separated by a crash.
How do you scale pulls?
Partition the change log by tenant, read with an index on (tenant_id, seq), cap pages by bytes, serve snapshots from a CDN for new devices, and push hints so devices pull only when something changed.

title: How an LLM works inside

labels.seq: Generating a reply token by token

summary: A large language model is a function that takes a sequence of tokens and returns a probability for every possible next token. Generation repeats that function, appending one chosen token at a time. Almost every engineering concern, from latency and cost to hallucination and context limits, follows from this loop.
does: Text becomes tokens; cost and limits are counted in tokens
Each layer mixes information between tokens (attention) and transforms it (MLP)
Prefill reads the whole prompt at once; decode writes one token per step
The KV cache stores past keys and values so decode is not quadratic
Sampling settings shape the output, not the model’s knowledge
doesnt: The model does not look facts up; it predicts likely text
A bigger context window does not mean it uses all of it equally well
Temperature 0 is not a guarantee of identical output across providers or hardware
Tokens are not words; Hindi or code can cost more tokens per word than English
scenario: A user asks the booking assistant: “Move my massage to Friday evening.” The orchestrator builds a prompt of about 2,400 tokens: system instructions, tool definitions, the last few turns and retrieved facts.

The tokenizer turns that text into 2,400 integer IDs using a byte-pair-encoding vocabulary of roughly 100,000 to 200,000 entries. Each ID is looked up in an embedding table and becomes a vector of a few thousand numbers.

Prefill: all 2,400 vectors pass through every transformer layer in parallel. In each layer, attention lets every token weigh earlier tokens; the MLP transforms each position. The keys and values from every layer are saved in the KV cache. This step decides time to first token.

Decode: the final position produces a score (logit) for every token in the vocabulary. The sampler applies temperature and top-p and picks one token, perhaps a tool-call marker. That single token is fed back in, attending to the cached keys and values, and the loop repeats until a stop token. Each step decides the time per output token.
archNotes: Tokenizer
Byte-pair encoding splits text into frequent sub-word pieces. Token counts drive price, latency and context limits, so always measure them with the provider’s tokenizer.
Self-attention

Each token produces a query, key and value. Scores are queries times keys, scaled by √d, turned into weights by softmax, and used to mix values. Causal masking stops a token from seeing the future. Grouped-query attention shares keys and values across heads to shrink the KV cache.
MLP and mixture of experts
A feed-forward network transforms each position independently. In mixture-of-experts models, a router sends each token to a few expert MLPs, so only part of the parameters run per token.
Positions
Rotary position embeddings (RoPE) encode order inside attention; context-extension techniques stretch them to longer windows.
KV cache
Saved keys and values for every past token in every layer. It makes decoding linear instead of quadratic, and it is the main memory cost of serving long prompts.
Sampler
Temperature rescales logits; top-p keeps the smallest set of tokens whose probability adds up to p. Lower values make output more predictable, not more correct.
states: A sub-word unit. Roughly ¾ of an English word on average; varies by language and content.
Maximum tokens of prompt plus output the model accepts in one call.
Reading the prompt in parallel / generating one token per step.
Raw scores over the vocabulary before sampling.
Learned weights; 7B, 70B and so on. Memory ≈ parameters × bytes per weight.
Learning to predict text at scale / then tuning to follow instructions and preferences.

msgs: Decode loop: one token per step

seqNotes: Prefill is compute-bound and grows with prompt length; long prompts mean slower first tokens.
Decode is memory-bandwidth-bound: each step reads all weights and the KV cache to produce one token.
This is why output tokens usually cost more than input tokens, and why streaming improves perceived speed.
code: Attention in a few lines (TypeScript, one head)
KV cache size for any model

bytes per token = 2 (K and V) × layers × kv_heads × head_dim × bytes_per_value
Llama-3-70B-class: 2 × 80 × 8 × 128 × 2 bytes ≈ 0.33 MB per token at FP16
4,000-token conversation ≈ 1.3 GB of GPU memory, per request
platforms: Cost and latency
You pay per input and output token; output tokens are slower and usually pricier.
Long system prompts cost on every call unless the provider caches the prefix.
Quality
Models attend unevenly over long contexts; put the most important instructions and facts near the start or end, and retrieve rather than paste everything.
Sampling settings change style and variance; evaluation decides them, not intuition.
Capacity planning
GPU memory = weights + KV cache; KV cache grows with concurrent users × context length.
Throughput depends on batching many decodes together.
tech: Dense vs mixture of experts
Dense: every parameter runs per token. MoE: a few experts per token
MoE gives large-model quality at lower compute per token, at the cost of more memory.
Context length
8k · 32k · 128k · 1M tokens
Longer windows simplify prompts but cost more and do not replace retrieval for large corpora.
Reasoning models
Spend extra tokens thinking before answering
Better on multi-step problems; slower and more expensive per answer.
Open vs hosted
Llama, Mistral, Gemma, Qwen families · hosted frontier models
Open weights for control and residency; hosted for top quality and no infrastructure.
metrics: Driven by prompt length and queueing.
Driven by model size, batch size and memory bandwidth.
How much of the window you actually send; trimming it is the easiest saving.
edges: The model predicts plausible text; ground answers with retrieval and tool results.
Instruction ignored in a long prompt
Too much context dilutes attention; shorten and restructure.
Hit max output tokens; raise the limit or ask for shorter structure.
Sampling randomness and batching effects; lower temperature and evaluate on sets, not single runs.
interview: Why does a long prompt slow the first token but not later tokens as much?
Prefill processes all prompt tokens at once, which is compute-heavy. Later tokens reuse the KV cache and only process one new position each.
What is the KV cache and why does it matter for serving?
Stored keys and values for past tokens in every layer. It avoids recomputation, but its memory grows with context and concurrency, so it limits how many users a GPU can serve.
What does temperature actually change?
It sharpens or flattens the probability distribution before sampling. It changes variety, not knowledge.
Why can Hindi text cost more than English?
Tokenizers are trained mostly on English, so other scripts split into more tokens per word.

title: Making inference fast and cheap
summary: Inference speed and cost come down to three limits: GPU compute during prefill, memory bandwidth during decode, and memory capacity for weights and KV cache. Every acceleration technique relaxes one of them: smaller numbers, fewer tokens, better batching, or guessing ahead.
does: Route easy requests to smaller models
Send fewer tokens: trim context, cache prefixes
Quantise weights and KV cache
Batch continuously and page the KV cache
Decode speculatively with a draft model
Distil a big model into a small task model
doesnt: Adding GPUs to a decode-bound workload without more batching
Raising max tokens ‘just in case’
Optimising before measuring TTFT, TPOT and cost per request
Quantising without re-running your evaluation set
scenario: A support summariser on a self-hosted 70B model costs too much and p95 latency is 9 seconds. The team measures first: average prompt 6,000 tokens, output 250, GPU utilisation 35% because requests are processed one at a time per replica.

Step one moves to vLLM with continuous batching and paged KV cache: throughput per GPU roughly triples and p95 drops, because the GPU now decodes many requests per step. Step two trims the prompt: ticket history is summarised once and cached, cutting input to 2,500 tokens and halving TTFT.

Step three quantises to FP8 weights and KV cache after the evaluation set shows less than 0.5% quality change, freeing memory for more concurrent requests. Step four routes short tickets to an 8B model distilled on the 70B model’s best summaries; 60% of traffic moves there.
Result: cost per summary falls by a large multiple and p95 latency drops below 3 seconds. Every step was gated on the same evaluation set and the same latency dashboard.
archNotes: Routing and distillation
The cheapest token is one processed by a smaller model. Classify requests and send routine ones to a small model, often distilled from the large one on your task.
Context trimming and caching
Input tokens dominate cost for retrieval-heavy apps. Summarise history, retrieve only relevant chunks, and keep stable prefixes identical so provider prompt caching or engine prefix caching applies.
Continuous batching
Instead of waiting for a batch to finish, the server adds and removes requests every decode step, keeping the GPU full.
Paged KV cache
vLLM’s PagedAttention stores KV cache in fixed-size blocks, like virtual memory, so long and short requests share memory without fragmentation.
FlashAttention
Exact attention computed in tiles that fit in fast on-chip memory, reducing slow memory reads; standard in modern engines.
Quantisation
Store weights (and optionally KV cache) in 8 or 4 bits. FP8 on recent GPUs keeps quality close to FP16; INT4 methods such as AWQ and GPTQ shrink further with more risk.
Speculative decoding
A small draft model proposes several tokens; the large model checks them in one forward pass and keeps the accepted prefix. Output quality is unchanged; speed rises when drafts are often right.
states: Reuse computed KV for a repeated prompt start, such as a long system prompt.
Return a stored answer for a sufficiently similar past question; only for stable, non-personal answers.
Asynchronous bulk processing at a discount from major providers, for work that can wait hours.
Split each layer across GPUs for big models; needs fast interconnect such as NVLink.
Run prefill and decode on separate GPU pools; useful at very large scale.

msgs: One expensive pass produced 4 tokens instead of 1

seqNotes: Speed-up depends on the acceptance rate, which is high for predictable text such as code and templated answers.
Because the target model verifies every token, the output matches what it would have produced on its own.
code: Serving with the main levers on (vLLM)

const route = (req: Req) =>
  req.tokens < 800 && classifier.isRoutine(req.intent) ? 'small-8b'
  : req.needsTools || req.tokens > 6000 ? 'large-70b'
  : 'medium';

const res = await llm.generate({ model: route(req), messages, maxTokens: 300 });   // cap output too
platforms: Hosted APIs
Model choice and routing are your biggest levers.
Prompt caching and batch APIs reduce cost for repeated prefixes and offline work.
Cap max output tokens and ask for concise structures.
Self-hosted GPUs
Continuous batching, paged KV cache and prefix caching through vLLM, SGLang or TensorRT-LLM.
FP8 quantisation on recent GPUs; tensor parallelism sized by memory.
Autoscale on queue depth and KV utilisation.
On device
Small models, 4-bit quantisation and hardware delegates (GPU, Neural Engine, NPU).
Short prompts and short outputs; cache results locally.
tech: Serving engines
vLLM · SGLang · TensorRT-LLM · Hugging Face TGI · llama.cpp
vLLM or SGLang for general GPU serving; TensorRT-LLM for maximum NVIDIA performance; llama.cpp for CPU and edge.
Quantisation
FP8 · AWQ · GPTQ · GGUF (llama.cpp)
FP8 first on supported GPUs; INT4 when memory is the hard limit.
Kernels
FlashAttention · fused kernels in engines
Usually provided by the engine; check versions match your GPU.
Distillation and fine-tuning
LoRA on a small model using large-model outputs
When a narrow task is high volume and quality can be measured.
metrics: TTFT and TPOT, p50 and p95
Cost per request and per successful task
Show whether prompt structure is cache-friendly.
Quality score on the eval set
edges: Evaluate per task, not on generic benchmarks; keep a higher-precision fallback.
Semantic cache serves a stale or personal answer
Cache only public, stable answers with TTLs; include version in the key.
Cap batch size or tokens per step to protect p95.
Escalate when the small model’s confidence or validation fails.
interview: Your LLM feature is too slow. Where do you start?

Measure TTFT versus TPOT. Slow first token means long prompts or queueing: trim context, cache prefixes, add capacity. Slow streaming means decode limits: batching, quantisation, speculative decoding or a smaller model.
Why does continuous batching help so much?
Decode is memory-bandwidth bound; reading the weights once to produce tokens for many requests amortises that cost.
Does speculative decoding change outputs?
No. The target model verifies every proposed token, so the result matches what it would have generated alone; only speed changes.
How do you cut cost by 10× without hurting quality?
Route most traffic to a small or distilled model, trim and cache context, cap outputs, batch offline work, and prove quality on an evaluation set at every step.

title: Embeddings and vector search

labels.scenario: Building semantic search for a service catalogue

summary: An embedding model turns text, images or audio into a vector so that similar meanings land close together. Vector search finds the nearest vectors quickly using approximate indexes. Together they power semantic search, recommendations, deduplication and the retrieval half of RAG.
does: Search by meaning instead of exact words
Compare across languages with multilingual models
Cluster, deduplicate and recommend
Feed relevant context to an LLM
doesnt: Exact identifiers such as SKUs, error codes and names
Negation and fine-grained constraints (“not vegan”)
Freshness unless you re-embed on change
Permissions unless you filter inside the query
scenario: The wellness app has 40,000 services across 3,000 clinics. Keyword search fails on ‘something for a stiff neck after long flights’ because no listing contains those words.

Each service is embedded from a short document: title, category, description and benefits. Vectors of 768 dimensions are stored in Postgres with pgvector and an HNSW index, alongside city, price and clinic ID for filtering.

A query is embedded with the same model, then searched twice: vector nearest neighbours and BM25 keyword search, both filtered by city. Results are merged with reciprocal rank fusion and the top 30 reranked by a cross-encoder.

Offline evaluation on 300 labelled queries shows recall at 10 rising substantially over keyword search, and bookings from search improve in an A/B test. Embeddings are recomputed only when a service description changes.
archNotes: Embedding model
Maps input to a fixed-length vector. Use the same model, version and preprocessing for documents and queries; changing models means re-embedding everything.
Similarity
Usually cosine similarity, or dot product on normalised vectors.
Approximate index
HNSW builds a navigable graph for fast, high-recall search; IVF partitions vectors into clusters; product quantisation compresses vectors to save memory at some recall cost.
Hybrid search
Keyword search catches exact terms; vector search catches meaning. Reciprocal rank fusion combines ranked lists without tuning score scales.
Reranker
A cross-encoder reads the query and each candidate together and scores relevance much more accurately, but is too slow to run on the whole corpus.
states: Compare against every vector. Perfect recall; fine up to around 100k vectors.
Graph index; fast and accurate; uses more memory; supports incremental inserts.
Cluster-based; cheaper to build; tune the number of clusters probed.
Compressed vectors; large memory savings with some recall loss.
Models trained so vectors can be truncated to fewer dimensions with graceful quality loss.

msgs: kNN top 50 + BM25 top 50, city filter

seqNotes: Filters run inside both searches so results never include other cities.
The reranker is where most of the precision comes from.
code: Recall at k for your own test set (TypeScript)
platforms: Inside your existing database
pgvector, OpenSearch k-NN or Elasticsearch: one system, transactional updates, easy filters.
Good into tens of millions of vectors with tuning.
Dedicated vector database
Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, Milvus: built for very large indexes, multi-tenancy and fast filtered search.
Adds another system to operate and keep in sync.
On device
Small embedding models and a local index for offline semantic search over a user’s own data.
Keeps private data on the phone.
tech: Embedding models
Hosted embedding APIs · open models (e.g. BGE, E5, multilingual variants)
Benchmark on your queries; check multilingual quality, dimension and cost.
Vector stores
pgvector · OpenSearch · Qdrant · Weaviate · Milvus · Pinecone
Start in the database you run; move when scale or filtering demands.
Rerankers
Cross-encoder models · hosted rerank APIs
Almost always worth it for top-k quality.
Evaluation
Labelled query sets · recall@k · nDCG
Without labels you cannot compare models or settings.
metrics: Did the right items make the candidate list?
Are the best items near the top?
Index parameters trade speed for recall.
edges: All vectors must be re-embedded; keep model_version on every row and dual-write during migration.
Hybrid search with BM25 fixes it.
Filtered search returns too few results
Increase candidate pool or use an index with native filtering.
Chunk by structure; long inputs blur meaning.
interview: Why combine keyword and vector search?
Vectors miss exact tokens like product codes; keywords miss paraphrases. Fusion gets both, and a reranker sorts the final list.
HNSW or IVF?
HNSW for high recall and incremental updates with enough memory; IVF with PQ when memory is tight and the index is rebuilt in batches.
How do you pick an embedding model?
Label a few hundred real queries, measure recall@k and latency for candidates, check language coverage and cost, then decide.

title: Prompting, RAG or fine-tuning?
summary: There are three main ways to make a general model fit your product: better prompts, retrieval of your data at query time, and changing the model’s weights. They solve different problems. Prompts and retrieval change what the model sees; fine-tuning changes how it behaves.
does: Prompting: format, tone, rules and few-shot examples
RAG: facts that change, citations and permissions
Fine-tuning: consistent style, narrow tasks, lower latency with a smaller model
Preference tuning: choosing between acceptable answers the way your users prefer
doesnt: Fine-tuning to teach facts that change weekly
RAG for behaviour the model should always show
Skipping evaluation because the demo looked good
Training on data you are not allowed to use
scenario: Feature one, a refund-policy assistant, needs current facts with citations and permissions. That is retrieval: policies change and must be quoted. Fine-tuning would freeze yesterday’s policy into weights.

Feature two, ticket classification into 40 categories at 2 million tickets a day, needs speed and low cost more than broad reasoning. A small model fine-tuned with LoRA on 20,000 labelled tickets matches the large model’s accuracy on this task at a fraction of the cost.

Feature three, marketing copy in a strict brand voice, first gets a strong system prompt with examples. When reviewers still edit a third of outputs, the team collects pairs of preferred and rejected drafts and applies preference tuning (DPO) to an open model.
All three share one evaluation harness, so each decision is backed by numbers rather than impressions.
archNotes: Start at the left
Each step right costs more data, more engineering and more maintenance. Move right only when evaluation shows the previous step is not enough.
Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)
Train on input → ideal output pairs. Good for formats, classification, extraction and a consistent voice.
LoRA and QLoRA

Train small low-rank adapter matrices instead of all weights. QLoRA does this on a 4-bit quantised base model, so large models can be tuned on modest GPUs. Many adapters can share one base model in serving.
Preference tuning
DPO learns directly from pairs of preferred and rejected answers. RLHF trains a reward model and optimises against it; more complex, used by model providers.
Distillation
Generate high-quality outputs with a large model, then fine-tune a small model on them for a narrow task.
states: Update all weights. Highest flexibility, highest cost and risk of forgetting.
Add trainable low-rank matrices to attention and MLP layers; typically well under 1% of parameters.
LoRA on a 4-bit base; fits large models on fewer GPUs.
Preference pairs, no separate reward model.
Hosted APIs that fine-tune supported models on uploaded examples.

msgs: score vs baseline on test set
Promote only if it beats prompting + RAG

seqNotes: Hold out a test set that the model never sees, and compare against the cheapest baseline, not just the original prompt.
Version the dataset, base model and adapter together.
code: LoRA in numbers: what you actually train (TypeScript)

{ "messages": [
  { "role": "system", "content": "Classify the support ticket. Reply with one category id." },
  { "role": "user", "content": "I was charged twice for my annual plan" },
  { "role": "assistant", "content": "billing.duplicate_charge" } ] }
platforms: Prompting
A versioned system prompt, 3–10 good examples, an evaluation set.
RAG
Clean, chunked documents with metadata and permissions; labelled questions for retrieval evaluation.
Fine-tuning
Thousands of high-quality input/output pairs representative of production; a held-out test set.
Preference tuning
Pairs of better and worse answers, ideally from real reviewer edits.
tech: Training libraries
Hugging Face Transformers · PEFT · TRL · Axolotl · Unsloth
PEFT + TRL for LoRA, SFT and DPO; Unsloth or Axolotl for fast recipes.
Hosted fine-tuning
Fine-tuning APIs from major providers and cloud platforms
When you want no training infrastructure and the base model is supported.
Serving adapters
vLLM multi-LoRA · TGI
Serve many adapters on one base model.
Experiment tracking
Weights & Biases · MLflow
Version data, configs, metrics and checkpoints.
metrics: Task accuracy / F1 on held-out test
Fine-tuning can degrade other skills; test them.
Often the reason to fine-tune a small model.
edges: Facts baked into weights go stale
Use retrieval for anything that changes.
Redact before training; models can memorise.
Diverse examples, held-out evaluation, early stopping.
Adapters are tied to a base; plan to retrain.
interview: When would you fine-tune instead of RAG?
When the problem is behaviour, format or cost on a narrow, high-volume task, not missing facts. Facts that change belong in retrieval.
What is LoRA and why is it popular?
It freezes the base model and trains small low-rank matrices, so training is cheap, adapters are small files, and many adapters can share one base in serving.
How do you know fine-tuning helped?
Compare against the best prompt + RAG baseline on a held-out test set, including cost and latency, and check for regressions on other skills.

title: Tool use, agents and MCP

labels.doesnt: What they should not do unsupervised

summary: Tool use lets a model call functions you define: it outputs a structured request, your code runs it, and the result goes back into the conversation. An agent is a loop of that pattern with a goal. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardises how AI applications connect to tools and data, so one integration works across many AI clients.
does: Look up live data through APIs
Take actions such as creating tickets or bookings
Plan multi-step tasks and recover from errors
Work across systems through standard MCP servers
doesnt: Irreversible or costly actions without human confirmation
Act with more permissions than the user who asked
Trust instructions found inside tool results or documents
Loop without limits on steps, time and cost
scenario: An on-call engineer asks the internal assistant: ‘Why did checkout errors spike at 14:00, and open an incident if it’s still happening?’ The assistant is an MCP host connected to MCP servers for metrics, logs, the deploy system and the incident tool.

The model calls metrics.query and sees errors rising at 13:58. It calls deploys.list and finds a payments-service release at 13:55, then logs.search for that service and finds a timeout to the payment provider introduced by a config change.

Errors are still elevated, so it proposes incidents.create with a summary, links and severity. Because creating an incident pages people, the host shows a confirmation card. The engineer approves; the incident opens with the evidence attached.
Every tool call, its arguments and results are traced. The agent had read-only access to metrics and logs and write access only to incidents, scoped to the engineer’s own permissions.
archNotes: Tool calling

You describe tools with names, descriptions and JSON schemas. The model returns a tool call with arguments; your code executes it and returns the result as a message. The model never runs code itself.
Agent loop
Repeat: send messages and tools to the model, execute any tool calls, append results, stop when the model answers or a limit is hit. Limits on steps, time and tokens are mandatory.
MCP

An open protocol introduced by Anthropic in late 2024 and adopted widely since. A host application runs MCP clients that connect to MCP servers. Servers expose tools (actions), resources (data to read) and prompts (templates). Messages use JSON-RPC 2.0 over local stdio or HTTP-based transports.
Why MCP matters
Without a standard, every AI app writes custom integrations for every system. With MCP, a team writes one server for its system and any MCP-capable client can use it.
Policy and approvals
Read tools run freely within the user’s scope; write tools need confirmation; destructive tools may be excluded entirely.
states: A callable function with a schema, e.g. create_incident.
Readable context exposed by a server, e.g. a release record or file.
The AI application / its connector to one server / the integration exposing capabilities.
Workflows follow fixed steps with LLM calls inside; agents choose their own steps. Prefer workflows when steps are known.
seqNotes: The host, not the model, decides whether a call needs approval.
Tool results are data; instructions inside them must not be followed blindly.
platforms: Design rules
Start with a workflow; promote to an agent only when steps genuinely vary.
Few, well-described tools beat many overlapping ones.
Return compact, structured tool results; truncate large outputs.
Security
Run tools with the end user’s permissions, never a super-user.
Require confirmation for writes; block destructive tools.
Treat tool output as untrusted input (prompt injection).
Operations
Trace every step with arguments, results, tokens and cost.
Evaluate on scripted tasks with expected tool trajectories.
tech: Protocols
MCP (tools, resources, prompts) · provider tool-calling APIs
MCP to expose systems once for many clients; direct tool calling inside a single app.
Agent frameworks
Provider agent SDKs · LangGraph · LlamaIndex · plain code
Plain code for simple loops; a framework when you need state machines, retries and persistence.
MCP servers
Official SDKs (TypeScript, Python, others) · existing servers for GitHub, databases, docs
Wrap internal APIs as servers owned by the teams that own the APIs.
Coding agents
Claude Code and similar terminal or IDE agents
Agents that read code, run commands and edit files under developer supervision.
real: Anthropic
Introduced MCP as an open standard in November 2024, with SDKs and reference servers.
Industry adoption
Through 2025, major AI platforms and developer tools added MCP client support, making it a common way to connect assistants to tools.
metrics: Did the agent achieve the goal on the evaluation set?
Points to unclear tool descriptions or flaky APIs.
How often humans accept proposed actions.
edges: Prompt injection via a ticket or web page
Untrusted content cannot authorise actions; writes need user confirmation.
Step, time and cost limits; detect repeated identical calls.
Scope tokens per user and per server; least privilege.
Paginate and summarise in the server; truncate in the host.
interview: What is MCP and why would you adopt it?

An open protocol for connecting AI applications to tools and data through servers that expose tools, resources and prompts over JSON-RPC. Teams build one server per system and every MCP-capable client can use it, instead of N×M custom integrations.
Workflow or agent?
A workflow when the steps are known: cheaper, testable, predictable. An agent when the path depends on what it discovers. Many production systems are workflows with small agentic steps.
How do you make an agent safe?
Least-privilege tools scoped to the user, confirmation for consequential actions, limits on steps and cost, untrusted handling of tool output, full tracing, and evaluation on scripted tasks.

title: Integrating LLMs into products

labels.scenario: Adding AI to an existing app

summary: Most LLM features are ordinary software with one unreliable, slow, expensive dependency in the middle. The patterns that make them production-grade are the same ones you use for payments or search: a gateway, contracts, retries, fallbacks, caching, budgets and observability.
does: One internal gateway in front of all model providers
Versioned prompt templates with owners
Structured outputs validated against a schema
Streaming to the client with cancel
Fallback models and graceful degradation
Per-feature budgets and per-user limits
doesnt: Calling providers directly from mobile apps with embedded keys
Free-text parsing of model output with regex
Unbounded retries on a slow provider
Logging full prompts with personal data
Shipping prompt changes without an evaluation run
scenario: A product team wants to add three features in a quarter: listing description rewrite, review summaries and a support assistant. Instead of each team calling providers directly, the platform team ships an LLM gateway in two weeks.

The gateway authenticates internal callers, looks up the prompt template version for the feature, routes to the configured model, enforces JSON schemas on output, retries once on transient errors, falls back to a second provider, and records tokens and cost per feature.

Review summaries run nightly through the provider’s batch API at a lower price. Description rewrites stream to the mobile app over server-sent events. The support assistant uses tools through the same gateway.
When one provider has an outage, traffic moves to the fallback automatically. When cost spikes, the dashboard shows which feature and prompt version caused it.
archNotes: Gateway
One service owns provider keys, routing, retries, fallbacks, quotas and metering. Teams call a stable internal API instead of provider SDKs.
Prompt registry
Templates stored with versions and owners; features reference a version, and rollbacks are configuration.
Structured output
Ask for JSON that matches a schema, using the provider’s schema or tool features where available, then validate. Invalid output triggers one repair attempt, then a fallback.
Resilience
Timeouts sized to the feature, one retry with jitter for transient errors, circuit breakers per provider, and a fallback model or non-AI path.
Metering
Tokens, latency and cost per feature, prompt version and model; daily budgets with alerts.
states: Server-sent events from gateway to client; render in small batches; support cancel.
JSON schema in the request, validation on the response.
Second provider or smaller model; then a non-AI experience.
Offline jobs through batch APIs at lower cost.
Stable prefixes reused across calls for lower cost and latency.
seqNotes: Retries are bounded and fallback is automatic.
The caller receives the same schema whichever provider answered.
platforms: Mobile apps
Never embed provider keys; call your gateway with the user’s session.
Stream with SSE, render in batches, allow cancel and retry.
Cache results in SQLite; show something useful offline.
Web
Same gateway; stream with fetch and ReadableStream.
Disable submit while streaming to avoid duplicate calls.
Privacy
Redact personal data before logging; set provider data-retention options.
Region-pin traffic where residency rules apply.
tech: Gateways
In-house service · open-source LLM proxies · cloud AI gateways
In-house when you need custom policy; a proxy to start quickly.
Schemas
JSON Schema · Zod · Pydantic
Define once, use for prompts, validation and types.
Observability
OpenTelemetry · LLM tracing tools (e.g. Langfuse, LangSmith)
Trace prompts, outputs, tokens and cost per feature.
Cost controls
Batch APIs · prompt caching · routing · output caps
Combine; each alone is partial.
metrics: Error rate and fallback rate per provider
edges: Circuit breaker, fallback provider, then a non-AI path.
Pin model versions; re-run evaluations before switching.
Per-feature budgets and per-request token caps.
Redaction at the gateway; restricted access.
interview: Why put a gateway in front of LLM providers?
Central keys, routing, retries, fallbacks, quotas, metering and policy. Teams ship features faster and the company can switch models without touching every service.
How do you get reliable structured data from a model?
Schema in the request using provider features where available, validation on the response, one repair attempt, then a fallback.
How do you add an LLM to a mobile app safely?
The app calls your backend, never the provider. Stream responses, support cancel, cache results, and design a useful experience when the AI path fails.

title: Using AI to accelerate engineering teams

labels.scenario: Rolling out AI coding tools to 150 engineers

summary: As a principal engineer you will be asked how AI changes the way your teams build software, and how you would roll it out responsibly. The answer covers tools, workflow changes, guardrails, measurement and culture, not just which assistant to buy.
does: Reading and explaining unfamiliar code
Writing tests, migrations and boilerplate
Refactors with clear patterns across many files
First drafts of RFCs, runbooks and incident timelines
Reviewing diffs for common mistakes
Investigating failures with logs and traces
doesnt: Security-sensitive code without expert review
Architecture decisions without human ownership
Merging generated code nobody understands
Sending proprietary code to tools without an enterprise agreement
scenario: Leadership wants AI tools for 150 mobile and backend engineers. You start with a four-week pilot in two teams: one mobile, one backend, with an enterprise plan that keeps code private and disables training on company data.

Engineers use an IDE assistant for completion and chat, and an agentic coding tool such as Claude Code for multi-file changes: it reads the repo, runs Gradle and tests, and proposes diffs that engineers review. A repository-level instructions file captures conventions: module boundaries, test commands and banned APIs.
CI adds an AI review pass that comments on likely bugs and missing tests; humans still approve. Test-generation is targeted at the sync engine, where coverage was weakest.

You measure before and after: PR cycle time, change failure rate, escaped defects, and a short developer survey. Results are shared openly, including where the tools did not help, before expanding to all teams with a paved-road setup.
archNotes: Context is the multiplier
Assistants perform far better with repository instructions, architecture docs and access to internal docs through MCP. Treat that context as maintained infrastructure.
Agents for multi-step changes
Agentic tools can run builds and tests and iterate on failures. Keep them in sandboxes with the developer approving commands and diffs.
Human ownership
Every merged line has a human owner who understands it. AI review supplements, never replaces, human approval.
Same quality gates
Generated code passes the same lint, tests, security scanning and dependency checks as any other code.
states: Explain, refactor, generate with selected context.
Read the repo, run commands, edit files, iterate on test failures.
Query logs, metrics and traces in natural language.
seqNotes: The engineer defines done and owns the result.
CI and human review are unchanged; AI shortens the loop before them.
code: Repository instructions file (e.g. CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md)

# Mobile app conventions
- Kotlin, Jetpack Compose, Hilt. Feature modules: :feature:<name>:api and :impl.
- Never depend on another feature's :impl module.
- Database access only through Room DAOs in :core:db; every write in withTransaction.
- Run before proposing a change: ./gradlew :app:lintDebug testDebugUnitTest
- Sync engine changes need a fault-injection test in :core:sync:test.
- Do not add dependencies without asking.
AI review step in CI (GitHub Actions sketch)

name: ai-review
on: pull_request
jobs:
  review:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions: { pull-requests: write, contents: read }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: AI pre-review (comments only, never approves)
        run: ./scripts/ai-review.sh --diff origin/main...HEAD --rules .review-rules.md
platforms: Data and security
Enterprise agreements with no training on your code and clear retention terms.
Secrets scanning before any code leaves the machine; block tools on regulated repositories if needed.
Quality
Same CI gates for all code; stricter review on security-sensitive paths.
Track escaped defects and change failure rate for AI-heavy changes.
Culture
Share prompts, instructions files and good workflows in a guild.
Make it optional at first; publish results honestly.

For multi-file changes, test fixing and codebase exploration.
Review

Change failure rate and escaped defects
AI can increase PR volume; watch reviewer burnout.
Perceived productivity and where it helps.
edges: Smaller PRs, AI pre-review, clear ownership.
Tests first, fault injection for critical modules, careful review.
Tools with code-reference filters and enterprise terms.
Pairing, explain-before-merge, and code reading practice.
interview: How would you roll out AI coding tools across teams?
A measured pilot with enterprise controls, instructions files and shared workflows, the same quality gates, before/after metrics including failure rates, then an honest review before scaling.
How do you measure whether AI helps?
Delivery metrics such as cycle time and lead time, quality metrics such as change failure rate and escaped defects, review load, and developer surveys, compared with a baseline.
What would you never let an AI agent do?
Merge without human review, use production credentials, change security-sensitive code without an expert, or send proprietary code to an unapproved tool.
